analysis.one_liner: Directs the FCC to cap what companies can charge families for phone calls from prison.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and died there when the Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: Phone calls from prison are among the most expensive in America — companies can charge families about $1 per minute plus $3 to connect each call, in part because prisons give one company an exclusive contract in exchange for a cut of the revenue, a fee that can reach 60 percent of what families pay. This bill directed the FCC to consider capping those rates and per-call fees, banning the commissions, and requiring prisons to allow competing phone providers. It never received a hearing or a vote and died when the 113th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Families of incarcerated people — disproportionately low-income households, since the person receiving the collect call pays the bill — would benefit from capped per-minute and per-call charges, a ban on the commissions baked into rates, and the option of cheaper debit-account and competing-provider service. The bill's own findings link cheaper calls to lower recidivism, a broader public benefit [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Families paying for calls from prison

how_it_helps.text: Directs the FCC to consider capping the per-minute and per-call charges companies can impose for prison phone calls, which today can reach about $1 per minute plus $3 per call.

Would prohibit the commissions phone companies pay to prison administrators for the exclusive right to serve a facility — payments that can account for as much as 60 percent of the revenue from prison phones and are built into the rates families pay.

Would require prisons to allow more than one phone provider so prisoners' families could choose a cheaper service, and require providers to offer both collect calling and cheaper debit-account options.

The bill's findings state that frequent family contact reduces recidivism and that high call rates burden or prevent that contact, so cheaper calls were framed as reducing future crime and prison costs.

analysis.who_pays: Prison phone companies would lose the high rates and the exclusive-contract commissions that make up their revenue; state and local correctional agencies would lose commission income of up to 60 percent of prison-phone revenue, which some facilities use to fund programs [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Prison phone companies and prison agencies

drawbacks.text: Banning the commissions phone companies pay to prisons would take away revenue that some state and local correctional agencies use to fund inmate programs, services, and facility operations — a real budget hit those agencies would have to replace from tax funds or cuts.

Capping per-minute and per-call rates while requiring providers to offer both collect and debit calling could reduce what carriers earn on a small, high-cost niche market, and critics could argue rigid rate caps risk under-funding the security features (like call monitoring) that prisons require.

The bill was written as a directive for the FCC to 'consider' various regulatory options in rulemaking, so even if enacted, the specific relief families would receive depended on how the commission drafted its rules.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits were large and concrete: the record shows per-minute rates near $1 and per-call charges of $3 [S3], paid by families who could least afford it, and the bill's own findings document that high rates erode the family contact that reduces recidivism [S3]. The costs fall on prison phone companies and on state/local agencies that would lose commission revenue — and it is fair to note that some facilities use that revenue to fund inmate programs, so replacing it requires a budget decision by states and counties. The bill directed the FCC to consider a menu of regulatory options rather than dictating specific rates, which limited the risk of bad design. On balance, the relief it targeted was badly needed; its fate meant none of it happened through this bill.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Communications subcommittee and never got a hearing, a vote, or a floor action before the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Rep. Bobby Rush introduced the bill on March 25, 2013, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
Four days later it was referred to the Communications and Technology subcommittee, which is where it stayed.
No further action appears in the record before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015, so the bill expired.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Prison phone companies and the state and local agencies that collect commissions from them kept charging the high rates and taking the commission payments the bill would have ended.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Prison phone companies and prison agencies

for.name: Rep. Bobby L. Rush
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and its findings that high prison phone rates burden low-income families and weaken reentry.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never held a markup or advanced it, leaving it in subcommittee until the Congress ended.

against.name: Prison phone industry
against.what_they_did: The companies that hold exclusive prison phone contracts have long opposed rate caps and commission bans through lobbying and litigation, defending a revenue model the bill targeted.

sides.party_line_note: All 12 supporters in the record — the sponsor and 11 cosponsors — were House Democrats, and the bill never advanced far enough for a vote that would show how the rest of the chamber would have split.

industries.industry: Prison phone companies (inmate telephone service providers)
industries.note: The bill would cap the per-minute and per-call rates these companies charge and ban the commissions they pay for exclusive facility contracts — the two main drivers of their high margins. Their interest ran directly against the families paying the rates.
These agencies collect commissions of up to 60 percent of prison-phone revenue for granting exclusive contracts; the bill would ban those payments and end that revenue stream.
